title: Overfitting and the generalization gap
prompt: Training accuracy is 100%, but test accuracy is 46%. Which proposed remedy is least common: L2, changing tanh to sigmoid, a smaller network, or BatchNorm?
answer: B · Replacing tanh with sigmoid is not a standard overfitting remedy.
steps: The network fits the training set perfectly but makes many mistakes on unseen examples. This is consistent with overfitting, although a distribution shift or a bad split could also create a gap.

L2 adds a cost for large weights; a smaller model limits capacity. Both can discourage memorizing training-specific details. BatchNorm can introduce a useful regularizing effect during training, although it does not guarantee better generalization.

Tanh and sigmoid both saturate. Swapping one for the other does not directly constrain model complexity or increase the training information. Choose changes using validation performance, then evaluate the final choice on test.
trap: A large gap is evidence to investigate, not a proof that every regularizer will help. B is the least standard remedy among these choices.
recall: Why might reducing capacity help here but hurt a model with high training error?
pages: 14–21, especially the model-complexity graph on p. 14; BatchNorm support on pp. 126–134
eli5: Think of a student who memorizes every practice-exam answer but struggles when the numbers change. Here, 100% training accuracy means the network gets every practice example right; 46% test accuracy means that success does not carry over to new examples. This is a classic overfitting pattern, assuming the data splits are comparable. Changing tanh to sigmoid does not directly stop memorization.
takeaway: High training accuracy and low held-out accuracy suggest overfitting. Consider regularization, less complexity, and more representative training data; choose changes using validation results.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Penalizes large weights, which can discourage fitting training-specific noise.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct choice for “least common remedy.” Changing these activations is not a standard way to reduce overfitting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduce the size of the neural network
choices.explanation: Limits capacity, making memorization harder; it can help an overfit model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Primarily helps training behavior and can also provide some regularization; it is not a guarantee.

teaching.heading: Why is changing the activation the odd one out?
teaching.example: Imagine 100 practice photos and 100 new photos. The model gets 100 practice photos right but only 46 new ones. Like memorizing a practice exam, it learned details that do not transfer well. A remedy should make memorization harder or provide better evidence—not simply swap two saturating activations.

comparison.does: Charges a cost for large weights
Changes the activation’s range and derivative

comparison.meaning: May also have a regularizing effect

remember: A large train–test gap suggests overfitting when the splits are comparable.
Regularization, less complexity, and more representative data can help.
Choose changes using validation data; do not repeatedly tune on test.

title: Max pooling and computation
prompt: Which layer is expected to use the fewest floating-point arithmetic operations: convolution plus bias, max pooling, sigmoid, or BatchNorm?
answer: B · Max pooling mainly compares values.
steps: A pooling window keeps its largest value. For [1, 7, 3, 2], three comparisons find 7; no learned dot product or exponential is required.
Convolution computes many multiplications and additions. Sigmoid computes 1/(1 + exp(−x)). BatchNorm performs centering, scaling, and usually a learned affine transformation.

This is an operation-count comparison under the intended comparable-layer setting. Actual wall-clock latency also depends on tensor sizes, memory traffic, hardware, and implementation. The question supplies no shapes that would establish a universal runtime ranking.
trap: Few arithmetic FLOPs does not mean zero work: comparisons, memory reads, and output writes still cost time.
recall: What operations does a 2×2 max pool perform, compared with a 2×2 learned filter?
pages: 73–85 (convolution and pooling calculations); 126–134 for BatchNorm arithmetic
eli5: A max-pooling layer is like finding the tallest person in a small group: compare heights and keep the winner. A convolution instead multiplies many numbers and adds them; sigmoid also needs an exponential, and BatchNorm needs centering and scaling. Max pooling therefore has the smallest arithmetic burden in the intended comparison.
takeaway: For an operation-count question, distinguish comparisons from multiply-adds, exponentials, and normalization. Actual runtime also depends on shapes and hardware.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Each output usually needs a learned dot product: many multiplications and additions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct. It mainly compares values within each window and keeps the maximum.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Computes an exponential and other arithmetic for each value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Centers, scales, and applies a learned scale and shift; this requires arithmetic.

teaching.heading: Why max pooling?
teaching.example: Imagine a 2×2 section of an image. Max pooling simply selects the largest value. It does not multiply learned weights or calculate an exponential. It compares numbers and keeps the biggest.

comparison.does: Multiply and add many pixel/filter values
Select the largest number in a window

remember: Convolution learns features using trainable filters.
Max pooling usually reduces spatial dimensions by selecting maxima.
Ordinary max pooling has zero trainable parameters.
Pooling is not mandatory in every CNN.

title: Zero initialization and gradient flow
prompt: All network parameters start at zero. After one forward/backward/update step, what can happen to the first-layer weights?
answer: Printed A is possible for some models; the question does not specify enough to make it universal.
steps: For a one-layer linear model, L = (wᵀx − y)² gives ∇w L = 2(wᵀx − y)x. At w = 0, the update is w ← 2ηyx. With y = 1 and x = (1, −1), the new weights are (2η, −2η), so both signs are possible.

For a conventional multilayer network, the first hidden-layer gradient contains the next layer’s weight matrix: δ₁ = (W₂ᵀδ₂) ⊙ g′(z₁). If W₂ = 0, then δ₁ = 0 on this first pass. Consequently W₁ remains zero after that simultaneous update: option D in this setting.

Even when identical hidden units later receive nonzero updates, symmetric units can remain identical. Random initialization breaks that symmetry; it is not a promise that every weight will have a particular sign.
trap: B and C impose an unjustified fixed sign. A needs an architecture that permits a nonzero first-layer gradient; zero initialization alone does not ensure that.
recall: Why can a zero-initialized linear regressor learn while an all-zero multilayer network can block its first-layer gradient?
note: Architecture-dependent key: A in the archive; D for the first update of a standard all-zero multilayer network.
eli5: Imagine a message passing backward through a chain of rooms. If the connection to an earlier room multiplies the message by zero, nothing reaches that room. That is what an all-zero downstream weight matrix does to the first hidden layer on the first update. A one-layer model has no such intermediate blockage and can update in either direction.
takeaway: A zero start does not determine an update’s sign. Check the architecture and the whole gradient path before accepting the archived A.

choices.label: A
choices.text: First-layer weights may be positive or negative
choices.explanation: Printed key. Possible for a one-layer linear model whose gradient depends directly on the input and target.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: No fixed negative sign follows from zero initialization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No fixed positive sign follows from zero initialization or “gradient direction.”

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: True for the first simultaneous update of a conventional all-zero multilayer network because the next weight matrix blocks the gradient.

teaching.heading: Why does the architecture change the answer?
teaching.example: In a single linear neuron with target 1 and input (1,−1), zero weights update to (2η,−2η). But put a zero-weight layer between the loss and the first hidden layer, and that backward signal is multiplied by zero. The first-layer weights then stay zero on that first update.

comparison.does: Its gradient can depend directly on x and y
comparison.meaning: The update can have either sign

comparison.does: The backward signal crosses a zero downstream matrix
comparison.meaning: First hidden-layer gradient is zero on the first pass
They may never learn different features

remember: An update is determined by its full gradient path.
Zero initialization does not imply one universal sign.
Random hidden-weight initialization helps break symmetry.

title: Parameters in one 1×1 filter
prompt: A 64×64 RGB image has 3 channels. How many weights does one standard 1×1 convolutional filter have, without bias?
answer: 3 weights.
steps: One output at a position combines the three input-channel values: y = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + w₃x₃.
Count kernel height × kernel width × input channels = 1×1×3 = 3. There is one output filter and no bias.
The same three weights are reused at all 64×64 locations. That produces many activations but does not add trainable parameters. With F such filters, the weight count would be 3F.
trap: Do not multiply by 64×64 when counting shared parameters. A 1×1 kernel still spans all input channels in a standard dense convolution.
recall: How would the count change with 8 output filters and one bias per filter?
eli5: A 1×1 RGB filter looks at one location through three colored windows: red, green, and blue. It needs one adjustable knob for each color. It reuses those same three knobs everywhere in the image.
takeaway: One standard filter has kernel height × kernel width × input channels weights. Image width and height do not multiply shared parameters.

teaching.heading: Why are there only three weights?
teaching.example: At one RGB pixel, let the three channels be (2,5,1) and the filter weights be (1,2,−1). The output is 1×2+2×5−1×1=11. Those same three weights are reused at the next pixel.

comparison.meaning: More uses of the weights, not more weights

remember: One filter spans all input channels in a standard convolution.
Parameter count is 1×1×3=3 without bias.
A separate output filter adds another set of weights.

title: Gradient norm clipping
prompt: Which listed method directly addresses exploding gradients? The last option rescales a gradient using a predefined norm threshold.
answer: D · Clip the gradient norm.
steps: An exploding gradient can produce an excessively large update Δθ = −ηg. Global norm clipping limits that update’s gradient magnitude before the optimizer uses it.
Use g_clipped = min(1, c/‖g‖₂)g for a positive threshold c. For g = (3,4) and c = 2, the norm is 5 and the clipped gradient is (1.2,1.6). Its direction is preserved.
Small SGD batches, oversampling minority classes, and increasing batch size address other concerns or change the noise of updates. None is the specific direct safeguard described here.
trap: The printed option letters are duplicated in the PDF. “D” refers to the fourth option about rescaling by the norm. Clipping does not enlarge small gradients.
recall: What happens to (0.03,0.04) if the clipping threshold is 1?
eli5: A huge gradient is like a direction arrow so long that one step sends you far past your destination. Norm clipping shortens the arrow when it exceeds a limit, while keeping its direction.
takeaway: Clipping caps large gradient norms; it does not amplify small gradients.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Changes gradient noise but does not directly cap an enormous gradient.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Addresses class imbalance, not exploding gradient magnitude.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increase batch size to reduce overfitting
choices.explanation: Does not directly bound gradients and does not inherently cure overfitting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rescale gradients above a norm threshold
choices.explanation: Correct. Shortens overly large gradients before the update. The PDF mislabels the last two option letters.

teaching.heading: Why does clipping stop an oversized update?
teaching.example: For gradient (3,4), the length is 5. With a length limit of 2, multiply both entries by 2/5. The result (1.2,1.6) points the same way but has length 2.

comparison.meaning: A large gradient can cause an oversized step

remember: Clipping is a ceiling on gradient size.
Use min(1,c/‖g‖) to avoid enlarging small gradients.
Clipping addresses explosion, not vanishing.

title: Decision-tree pruning
prompt: What is pruning primarily for: reducing depth and overfitting, L2 on tree parameters, handling missing data, or improving interpretability with a smaller tree?
answer: A · Reduce complexity to control overfitting.
steps: A fully grown tree can make branches for noise or isolated training examples. Removing weak subtrees or limiting depth prevents some training-specific distinctions.
The result may have higher training error but better validation and test performance. Choose pruning strength using validation or a suitable cross-validation procedure.

D, improved interpretability, is a genuine benefit of a smaller tree, but A identifies the main generalization motivation. B describes a different kind of penalty, and C is not the primary purpose of pruning.
trap: Pruning is not a guarantee of lower test error; excessive pruning can underfit. D is plausible, so “primary purpose” matters.
recall: Why should pruning depth be selected on validation error instead of training error?
eli5: An overgrown decision tree is like a rulebook with a special rule for every tiny exception. Pruning cuts some of those exceptions so the rules are more likely to work on new cases.
takeaway: Pruning reduces tree complexity to help generalization; select its strength on validation data.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduce tree depth and prevent overfitting
choices.explanation: Best answer. Removing weak branches reduces the ability to memorize training quirks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: L2 weight penalties are not the pruning operation described here.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Missing-value handling is a separate modeling issue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Improve interpretability with a smaller tree
choices.explanation: A real benefit, but the question’s primary statistical purpose is controlling overfitting.

teaching.heading: Why prune a decision tree?
teaching.example: Suppose a tree learns “this one unusual leaf shape means tulip” from a single noisy photo. Pruning can remove that fragile exception and use the broader rule above it. Training accuracy may fall while new-photo accuracy improves.

comparison.meaning: Trades some fit for a simpler rule
Helps choose how much simplification is useful

remember: Pruning controls complexity.
Simpler trees can generalize better and be easier to read.
Too much pruning can underfit.

title: RNN parameters becoming NaN
prompt: An RNN’s parameters become NaN. Which listed cause is most likely?
answer: B · Exploding gradients.
steps: Backpropagation through time multiplies recurrent Jacobians across many steps. If their product grows strongly, the gradients and subsequent parameter updates can become enormous.

Overflow can create infinity, and later operations such as infinity minus infinity can yield NaN. Clipping and inspecting learning rate, activations, loss, and numerical stability help diagnose the failure.

Vanishing gradients usually make updates too small. ReLU on a large finite positive number simply returns that number. A large sigmoid input mathematically saturates toward 1 rather than inherently producing NaN.
trap: NaN is not a unique signature: invalid input, unstable formulas, division by zero, or a large learning rate can also cause it. B is the best listed explanation.
recall: What would vanishing gradients look like during training compared with exploding gradients?
specificTopic: RNN numerical instability from exploding gradients
eli5: If you keep multiplying a number by something larger than one, it can grow until the computer cannot store it. RNN gradients can do that across time. Overflow and later invalid arithmetic can then turn weights into NaN.
takeaway: NaN suggests checking exploding gradients and numerical stability. Vanishing gradients usually cause tiny updates instead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usually make learning signals too small; they do not ordinarily overflow parameters.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Best listed cause. Huge updates can cause overflow and invalid arithmetic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: ReLU on a very large input
choices.explanation: For a finite positive input, ReLU simply returns that input; this alone does not explain NaN.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigmoid on a very large input
choices.explanation: Mathematically approaches 1; stable sigmoid implementations handle saturation without NaN.

teaching.heading: Why can exploding gradients produce NaN?
teaching.example: Repeated doubling gives 2,4,8,16,… . A long enough chain can exceed the largest number the computer can store. If later arithmetic combines infinities invalidly, such as infinity minus infinity, the result becomes NaN.
remember: Explosion is the best listed explanation, not the only possible NaN cause.
Check inputs, losses, learning rate, and gradient norms.
A large finite ReLU input alone is not a NaN mechanism.

title: L2 regularization in GNNs
prompt: Can ordinary neural-network regularization such as L2 be applied to graph neural networks?
answer: B · Yes, GNNs also learn weight parameters.
steps: A GNN learns matrices for message transforms, neighbor combinations, or prediction heads. A penalty λ∑wᵢ² can be added to its training objective just as in an MLP.
The existence of graph edges does not make that derivative invalid: the penalty contributes 2λwᵢ to each penalized weight’s gradient.

A confuses weight shrinkage with oversmoothing, which concerns node representations becoming too similar after repeated mixing. C incorrectly claims aggregation prevents L2. D introduces an unsupported general claim that early stopping replaces L2 in practice.
trap: Regularizing shared weights and choosing the number of message-passing layers address different mechanisms. Tune regularization using validation data.
recall: Which trainable quantities in a GNN could receive an L2 penalty?
eli5: A graph network still has adjustable weight knobs. L2 charges a cost for turning those knobs too far, just as it does in an ordinary neural network. Working with connected nodes does not remove those weights.
takeaway: Standard weight regularizers can apply to GNNs. Weight shrinkage and oversmoothing are different mechanisms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Incorrect. Oversmoothing is about node representations becoming alike, not simply weights being penalized.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct. Their shared matrices can receive the same kind of L2 penalty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No; L2 causes aggregation gradient errors
choices.explanation: Incorrect. A differentiable weight penalty can be combined with aggregation-based training.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Yes, but early stopping is generally used instead
choices.explanation: The “yes” is plausible, but the extra broad claim about replacing L2 is not established.

teaching.heading: Why does L2 still work on a graph?
teaching.example: A GNN might compute h=Wh_self+Uh_neighbors. W and U are still learned weight matrices. Adding λ(‖W‖²+‖U‖²) charges for large values just as in an ordinary network.

comparison.meaning: Controls a different mechanism from graph mixing

remember: Graphs change how examples communicate, not whether weights exist.
L2 adds a valid gradient to the objective.
Weight shrinkage is not the definition of oversmoothing.

title: Neighborhood aggregation
prompt: What is the primary purpose of the aggregation function in a GNN?
answer: A · Combine information from a node’s neighbors.
steps: For a target node v, collect messages from neighbors N(v). A sum, mean, max, or appropriately constructed attention aggregation converts that variable-size collection into a vector.
For neighbors with scalar values 2 and 4, a mean aggregator returns 3. The update then combines this neighbor information with the target node’s own representation.
Dimensionality reduction is not the defining purpose. Node classification and edge prediction are downstream tasks that may use the resulting embeddings.
trap: Separate aggregation, the node update, and the prediction head. An aggregate is not automatically a class label.
recall: How would adding a neighbor with value 9 change the mean aggregate of neighbors 2 and 4?
eli5: To understand one road, ask what is happening on nearby connected roads. Aggregation collects those neighbors’ messages into one summary that helps update the road’s representation.
takeaway: Aggregation summarizes neighbors; a later update or prediction head uses that summary.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combine neighbor information to update a node
choices.explanation: Correct. This is the defining neighborhood-message role.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Can happen in a design, but is not what defines aggregation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Classification is a task that may use the resulting embeddings.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Link prediction is another downstream task, not the definition of aggregation.

teaching.heading: What does aggregation actually do?
teaching.example: Road A is connected to roads with values 2 and 4. A mean aggregator reports 3. A later update might blend A’s own value 1 with that summary: 0.5×1+0.5×3=2.

comparison.meaning: Produces a class, score, or other task output

remember: Aggregation and prediction are different steps.
Mean, sum, and max can summarize neighbor sets.
The same aggregation rule is reused across nodes.

title: Are pooling layers required?
prompt: Must every CNN include pooling layers?
answer: C · No; pooling is commonly used for spatial reduction.
steps: Convolution supplies local receptive fields and parameter sharing. Neither property requires a separate pooling layer.

Pooling reduces spatial resolution and downstream computation. It can discard detail and sometimes reduce overfitting or add limited tolerance to small shifts. Strided convolutions can also perform downsampling.

A is wrong because convolution itself uses spatial neighborhoods. B is wrong because pooling is not required to prevent vanishing gradients. D mentions nonlinearity, but spatial reduction is the intended main role; average pooling is linear.
trap: Pooling is an architectural choice. Max pooling is nonlinear, but not every pooling operator is nonlinear or a generalization guarantee.
recall: How could a CNN reduce feature-map size without a pooling layer?
eli5: Pooling is like shrinking a large picture into a smaller summary. It can make the next layers cheaper, but a CNN can still read local patterns without this separate shrinking step.
takeaway: CNNs do not require pooling. It is mainly a downsampling choice; strided convolutions can also shrink feature maps.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Yes; pooling is needed to preserve spatial correlation
choices.explanation: Convolution itself reads local spatial neighborhoods.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Pooling is not a necessary cure for vanishing gradients.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No; it mainly reduces dimensionality and can help limit overfitting
choices.explanation: Best answer. Pooling is optional spatial reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Not its primary general role; average pooling is linear.

teaching.heading: Why is pooling optional?
teaching.example: An 8×8 feature map can become 4×4 using a 2×2 pool with stride 2. A strided convolution can also reduce its size. Neither choice is required for convolution to recognize local patterns.

comparison.does: Reads local neighborhoods with shared filters
Computes learned outputs at spaced positions

remember: Pooling is a design choice.
Downsampling reduces computation but can discard detail.
Max pooling is nonlinear; average pooling is linear.

title: Why ReLU is nonlinear
prompt: Why is ReLU nonlinear even though each of its two pieces is linear?
answer: C · Its slope changes at zero.
steps: ReLU(x) = max(0,x). Its slope is 0 for x < 0 and 1 for x > 0, so no single linear function describes it over the whole real line.
A direct linearity test gives ReLU(1 + (−1)) = 0, while ReLU(1) + ReLU(−1) = 1. Failure of additivity proves nonlinearity.

A incorrectly says it only outputs positive values; zero is possible. B describes only the nonnegative branch. D describes its piecewise form, but having two linear pieces alone is not a sufficient explanation: pieces with the same rule could form one global linear map.
trap: Piecewise linear and globally linear are different properties. The key fact is the different slopes, not just having a case distinction.
recall: Give another pair of inputs that violates additivity for ReLU.
eli5: A straight ramp keeps the same slope everywhere. ReLU is a flat floor for negative inputs and a rising ramp for positive inputs. The bend where they meet means one straight-line rule cannot describe the whole function.
takeaway: Piecewise linear does not mean globally linear. ReLU fails additivity because its slope changes at zero.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Not sufficient and not literally true: ReLU also outputs zero.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Only true on its nonnegative branch.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct. The two regions do not form a single global linear map.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Describes ReLU, but having pieces alone is not sufficient; the different slopes explain why the whole function is nonlinear.

teaching.heading: Why is a piecewise straight function nonlinear?
teaching.example: Use inputs 1 and −1. ReLU(1)+ReLU(−1)=1+0=1, but ReLU(1−1)=ReLU(0)=0. A linear function would have to give the same answer both ways.
remember: Piecewise linear is not the same as globally linear.
ReLU includes zero in its outputs.
The changing slope explains the nonlinearity.

title: Why hidden nonlinearities matter
prompt: Why do neural networks need nonlinear transformations between layers?
answer: C · They make nonlinear relationships representable.
steps: Two linear layers collapse: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. With biases, they still collapse to one affine map: W₂W₁x + W₂b₁ + b₂.
A nonlinearity between them prevents that general collapse. Different regions of input space can activate different hidden units, allowing the model to express more complicated boundaries.
A reverses the point by limiting the model to linear separation. B and D describe possible practical outcomes, not the fundamental increase in representational capacity.
trap: Adding depth without nonlinearities does not by itself create a nonlinear predictor. More parameters and more expressive function classes are not the same thing.
recall: Why can a wide stack of affine layers still fail to model an absolute-value function exactly over positive and negative inputs?
eli5: Stacking straight-line rules is like stacking transparent straight rulers: the result is still a straight-line rule. Nonlinear activations let the network bend its response and describe patterns that one affine map cannot.
takeaway: Without nonlinearities, stacked affine layers collapse into one affine layer.

choices.label: A
choices.text: They allow only linearly separable functions
choices.explanation: Reverses the purpose: nonlinearities allow more than linear relationships.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They mainly make binary classification more efficient
choices.explanation: Too narrow; nonlinearities matter for many kinds of tasks.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct. They expand the functions the network can represent.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Training speed is not their fundamental representational purpose.

teaching.heading: Why does depth need a nonlinearity?
teaching.example: Let the first layer give h=3x+2 and the next give y=2h−1. Substitution gives y=6x+3. Two affine layers became one. An activation between them can introduce a bend that substitution cannot eliminate.
remember: Depth alone does not guarantee a nonlinear predictor.
Nonlinearities expand representational power.
Hidden features need not be probabilities.

title: Weighted sum and linear activation
prompt: Inputs 1, 2, 3 have corresponding weights 4, 5, 6. Sum the weighted inputs, then multiply that sum by 3.
steps: Pair each input with its own weight: 1×4 = 4, 2×5 = 10, and 3×6 = 18.
Add the contributions: z = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. No bias is specified.
Apply the stated activation g(z) = 3z: g(32) = 96. The option 32 stops before the activation; 643 and 9 do not follow the described operations.
trap: “Linear activation” does not necessarily mean the identity: here its slope is explicitly 3.
recall: If the activation were g(z) = 2z and a bias of −2 were added before it, what would the output be?
specificTopic: MLP forward pass and weighted sums
eli5: Each input contributes its value times its importance: 1×4, 2×5, and 3×6. Add those contributions to get 32, then follow the final instruction to triple the result.
takeaway: Apply the operations in order: weighted products → sum → activation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Stops after the weighted sum and skips the stated activation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Does not follow the specified products and sum.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Does not account for the weights and final multiplication correctly.

teaching.heading: Why is the output 96 rather than 32?
teaching.example: First build the weighted sum: 1×4=4, 2×5=10, 3×6=18. These total 32. The activation then triples 32, giving 96.

remember: Respect the order of computation.
A linear activation can have a slope other than 1.
Do not stop before applying the stated activation.

title: Decision-tree overfitting
prompt: Which listed disadvantage of decision trees is valid?
answer: C · Decision trees are prone to overfitting.
steps: A deep tree can keep splitting until it isolates training examples, including noisy ones. Those branches may fail on new data.

Single small trees are often interpretable, so A’s blanket claim of lacking interpretability is false. Prediction follows one root-to-leaf path and does not usually compare against the full training set as basic kNN does, so B is not a general disadvantage.
Because A and B are not generally true, “all of the above” is also wrong. Depth limits, pruning, minimum leaf sizes, and ensembles can help control the problem.
trap: A tree can be highly interpretable and still overfit. Interpretability does not establish accuracy on unseen data.
recall: How can two trees have identical training accuracy but different test accuracy?
eli5: A tree can keep inventing narrower rules until each training example has its own special case. Those rules can describe the practice set perfectly while being unreliable on new cases.
takeaway: A deep single tree is prone to overfitting even though a small tree can be easy to interpret.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Small decision trees are often interpretable; this blanket statement is false.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Trees are costly to run compared with kNN
choices.explanation: Tree prediction usually follows one path rather than scanning all training examples.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct. Unrestricted branching can fit training noise.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect because the first two claims are not generally true.

teaching.heading: Why can a readable tree still overfit?
teaching.example: A rule such as “if this exact photo has this exact tiny mark, call it a cat” is easy to read but may be useless on new photos. Interpretability says you can inspect the rule, not that the rule generalizes.

comparison.does: How easily the rules can be inspected
How well the rules match seen examples
comparison.meaning: Can be perfect in a large tree

comparison.does: How well they work on new examples

remember: Readability and accuracy are different properties.
Unrestricted trees can memorize training noise.
Pruning and depth limits can control complexity.

title: Shared GNN parameters and graph size
prompt: How can a GNN accept graphs with different numbers of nodes and different connectivity?
answer: B · Reuse a fixed set of shared parameters.
steps: A typical layer applies the same feature transform and aggregation rule at every node. Its matrices depend on feature widths, not on the total number of nodes.
If each node has two features, a 2×2 shared transform can be applied to three nodes or a thousand nodes. The adjacency structure determines which messages are combined.

A and D describe possible batching or preprocessing choices, not the fundamental reason. C is unnecessary: more nodes do not inherently require more layers. Layers mainly control how far local information propagates.
trap: Feature definitions and widths must remain compatible. Being able to compute outputs on a new graph does not guarantee good predictive accuracy.

title: Graph autoencoders

title: Initialization versus regularization
prompt: Which is not normally classified as a regularization technique: pruning, L2, random initialization, or augmentation?
answer: C · Random weight initialization.
steps: Initialization chooses the starting parameter values. Different initial values let hidden units learn different features and can improve signal and gradient propagation.

Pruning reduces model complexity; L2 changes the objective to penalize large weights; augmentation provides transformed training examples with valid labels. These are standard ways of influencing generalization.
Initialization can affect the eventual solution and its generalization, but its usual role is enabling effective optimization. That distinction makes C the intended answer.
trap: Randomness alone does not make an operation regularization. Ask which mechanism it changes and why.
recall: How do random initialization and random dropout act at different stages of training?
eli5: Initialization is choosing where runners stand at the start. Regularization changes the training rules so the model is less tempted to memorize. Random starting weights help neurons learn different things, but are not usually classified as a regularizer.
takeaway: Initialization sets the starting point; pruning, penalties, and augmentation are standard regularization approaches.

title: Recognizing sigmoid
prompt: Among the five activation plots labeled A–E in the exam, which is sigmoid?
answer: E · The S-shaped curve from 0 to 1.
steps: The logistic sigmoid is σ(x) = 1/(1 + exp(−x)). It approaches 0 on the far left, equals 1/2 at x = 0, and approaches 1 on the far right.
Plot E has that range and midpoint. Plot D is also S-shaped, but it ranges from −1 to 1 and crosses (0,0), identifying tanh.
The other plots are A: ReLU, B: leaky ReLU, and C: ELU. Their positive sides keep rising rather than saturating at 1.
trap: Check the vertical scale as well as the shape. “S-shaped” alone does not distinguish sigmoid from tanh.
recall: What are sigmoid(0), tanh(0), and the two functions’ output ranges?
eli5: Look at both ends of the curve. Sigmoid turns very negative inputs into values near 0 and very positive inputs into values near 1, with 0.5 in the middle. That is curve E.
takeaway: Distinguish sigmoid from tanh using the output range and value at zero, not just the S shape.

title: Activation range and derivative
prompt: Which primary activation properties govern their use: range and slope, range alone, probability outputs alone, or probability outputs and slope?
answer: A · Both output range and response rate (derivative).

The derivative controls how gradients pass through it. Sigmoid’s derivative σ(x)(1−σ(x)) becomes small at saturated inputs; ReLU has slope 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative inputs.

title: BatchNorm in training and evaluation

title: RNNs can have both gradient problems
prompt: Which RNN statement is false? A claims RNNs have vanishing gradients but never exploding gradients.
answer: A · RNNs can suffer from both.
steps: Unroll the recurrent computation across time. A gradient from a late step to an early step contains a product of local Jacobians.

In a scalar toy recurrence with derivative a, a path over T links contributes aᵀ. For a=0.5 this shrinks; for a=2 it grows. Real networks use matrices and activation derivatives, but the repeated-product mechanism remains.

RNNs can process variable-length sequences by reusing one update rule and can emit an output at every step. Thus B and C are valid; D correctly identifies vanishing gradients as a training difficulty.
trap: Sequence length is the depth of the unrolled gradient path even if the model has only one recurrent layer.
recall: Why does gradient clipping help one of these two problems but not the other?
eli5: An RNN repeats the same update across time. The backward signal repeatedly gets multiplied too: many small factors can erase it, while many large factors can make it blow up.
takeaway: RNNs can suffer from both vanishing and exploding gradients.

title: Recovering a convolution kernel shape

title: Binary attributes and tree leaves
prompt: A tree learns from N examples with k binary attributes. What is the largest number of leaves among the listed choices?

steps: Each binary attribute has two values, so at most 2ᵏ distinct feature vectors exist. A full useful tree can ask each attribute once on a path, distinguishing one pattern at each leaf.
For k=3, there are 8 patterns, from 000 through 111. Eight nonempty leaves are attainable if all eight patterns appear and the split criterion permits the full tree.

On a finite dataset, each nonempty leaf needs at least one example. The tighter bound is min(N,2ᵏ), and for a specific dataset it is at most the number of observed distinct patterns. Duplicate feature vectors cannot be separated by feature tests.

title: Worst-case continuous-tree depth
prompt: For N examples with continuous attributes, what is the maximal possible depth?
steps: At each proper binary split along a path, at least one sample goes into the sibling branch. The largest possible continuing child therefore contains one fewer sample than its parent.
An extreme tree peels off one example at each split: N→N−1→N−2→…→1. It uses N−1 edges from root to deepest leaf.
The exam counts nodes after the root, including the leaf, which is also N−1 for this chain. A balanced tree has much smaller depth, near log₂N, but the question asks for the worst case.
trap: The bound assumes nonempty children and that growth is allowed. Balance is not guaranteed by the definition of a decision tree.
recall: Sketch a tree with 4 examples whose deepest leaf is at depth 3.
eli5: The most lopsided tree peels off one example at a time. Starting with N examples, it takes N−1 proper splits along the deepest path to leave the last example alone.
takeaway: Balanced depth can be logarithmic, but worst-case continuous-tree depth is N−1 under the exam’s convention.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Not the proper-split depth bound from N examples.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A continuous feature can be tested at multiple thresholds on the same path.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Correct. Each continuing split can remove just one example.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A feature-pattern expression does not give this sample-based chain depth.

teaching.heading: Why is the worst-case depth N−1?
teaching.example: For four ordered examples, split off the first, then the second, then the third. The last example ends three edges below the root. This is a chain, not a balanced tree.

comparison.meaning: Limits how long the chain can grow

remember: Worst-case depth is not balanced depth.
The bound assumes nonempty children.
Count depth using the stated root/leaf convention.

title: Which layers are nonlinear?
prompt: The archive asks which layer is not linear, listing convolution, pooling, ReLU, and BatchNorm.
answer: C · ReLU is definitely nonlinear, but the item is not uniquely correct as written.
steps: ReLU fails additivity because its slope changes at zero. This makes C the intended answer.

Pooling is underspecified. Fixed average pooling is linear, whereas max pooling is nonlinear: max(2,0)+max(0,3)=5, but max((2,0)+(0,3))=3. The 2026 review explicitly teaches this counterexample on page 83.

Convolution without bias is linear in its input; with bias it is affine. BatchNorm with frozen statistics is affine in its input, while training-mode BatchNorm depends on batch-derived statistics and is generally nonlinear as a map of the batch.
trap: If “pooling” means max pooling, B is also nonlinear. If “linear” is used in the strict mathematical sense, biases and BatchNorm’s mode matter too. Do not infer that parameter-free operations must be linear.
recall: Which of max pooling, average pooling, biased convolution, and training BatchNorm passes the strict linearity tests?
note: Key ambiguity: C is intended; max pooling is also nonlinear.
specificTopic: Layer linearity: ReLU, pooling, and BatchNorm
eli5: A linear rule must treat “add first” the same as “process separately, then add.” ReLU fails this test, but max pooling does too. The question only says “pooling,” so its printed single-answer key leaves out an important distinction.
takeaway: ReLU and max pooling are nonlinear. Average pooling is linear; biased layers are affine, and BatchNorm depends on its mode.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Linear in the input without bias; affine with bias.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ambiguous. Average pooling is linear, while max pooling is nonlinear.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Printed intended answer. Its changing slope makes it nonlinear.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Affine with fixed evaluation statistics, but generally nonlinear as a function of a training batch.

teaching.heading: Why is “which layer is nonlinear?” underspecified?
teaching.example: Max pooling fails a simple test: max(2,0)+max(0,3)=5, but max(2,3)=3. Thus max pooling is nonlinear too, even though it has no learned parameters.

comparison.does: Average adds; max selects a winner
comparison.meaning: Average is linear; max is not
Evaluation is affine; training is generally nonlinear

remember: The printed C is intended but not uniquely correct for max pooling.
No learned parameters does not imply linearity.
Biases and BatchNorm mode matter for strict terminology.

title: Does basic kNN learn weights?
prompt: There are 100 examples, each with 64 features. How many parameters must a basic 3-nearest-neighbor classifier learn?
answer: 0 learned model weights.
steps: Basic kNN stores the training feature vectors and labels. At prediction time it computes distances, finds the three nearest examples, and takes a label vote.
No gradient-based fitting of a weight matrix is required. The 100×64 stored feature values are data memory, not learned network weights.
The neighbor count k=3 is a hyperparameter selected by a protocol such as validation. A separately learned metric or embedding would add trainable parameters, but that is not part of basic kNN here.
trap: Zero learned weights does not imply zero storage, zero computation, or zero hyperparameters.
recall: Why can kNN have almost no fitting computation but very expensive prediction?
specificTopic: kNN learned parameters versus stored data
eli5: Basic kNN is like keeping a folder of labeled examples and consulting the three most similar ones. It remembers the examples rather than fitting a set of prediction weights.
takeaway: Basic kNN has zero learned model weights, but still stores data and has a chosen neighbor-count hyperparameter.

teaching.heading: Why does basic kNN learn zero weights?
teaching.example: Keep 100 labeled feature vectors in a folder. For a query, find the closest three and let their labels vote. The folder contains data; there is no fitted neural-network weight matrix.

comparison.meaning: Memory cost, not fitted model weights

remember: Stored data are not learned weights.
Zero learned weights does not mean zero computation.
A separately learned metric would change the model.

title: Convolution weights plus biases
prompt: A convolution has 3 filters, each shaped (channels,height,width)=(3,2,2). Count parameters including biases.
answer: 39 parameters.
steps: One filter needs 3×2×2 = 12 weights: all three channels across its 2×2 spatial window.
Add one bias for that output filter, giving 12+1 = 13 parameters per filter.
Three filters use 3×13 = 39 parameters: 36 weights and 3 biases. They create three output channels regardless of the number of spatial locations.
trap: There is normally one bias per output channel, not one bias per input channel or per output pixel.
recall: How many parameters would 5 filters of shape (3,2,2) use without biases?
eli5: Each filter has twelve adjustable weights: three channels times a 2×2 window. Give each filter one extra bias knob, then repeat for three filters.
takeaway: With biases, convolution parameters = output filters × (input channels × kernel area + 1).

teaching.heading: Why do three filters use 39 parameters?
teaching.example: One filter has 3×2×2=12 weights and one bias, totaling 13. There are three such filters, so 13+13+13=39.
remember: Count biases per output channel.
Output pixels reuse these parameters.
Input-channel count belongs inside each filter.

title: kNN inference on 100 billion images
prompt: For 100 billion RGB 224×224 training images, which listed trained predictor is expected to be least efficient at labeling a new image: 10-NN, AlexNet, ResNet-50, or the specified deep MLP?
answer: A · A basic 10-nearest-neighbor classifier.
steps: An image has 3×224×224 = 150,528 raw coordinates. Exact brute-force kNN evaluates a distance to each of N=10¹¹ training examples, then selects the nearest ten.
That makes the distance work scale roughly as N×D, about 1.5×10¹⁶ coordinate comparisons or differences per query before accounting for all arithmetic and data movement.

A fixed trained neural network applies a finite set of learned layers to the new input. Its forward-pass cost does not directly grow with the number of training examples, making basic kNN the intended least efficient choice at this scale.
trap: “10 nearest” limits the final vote to ten neighbors; it does not mean only ten candidates are searched. Indexes and approximate nearest-neighbor systems change the cost, but are not specified.
recall: Which part of basic kNN prediction grows when the training set doubles?
specificTopic: kNN inference complexity at large scale
eli5: Imagine answering a new question by comparing it with 100 billion examples before choosing ten neighbors. That is much more work than applying a fixed learned rule once.
takeaway: Basic exact kNN prediction scales with stored training-set size; a fixed neural network’s forward pass does not.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Correct. Basic exact search compares the new image against an enormous stored dataset.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Applies a fixed sequence of learned operations to the new image.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Also has a fixed forward-pass cost independent of training-set size.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: May be costly, but its inference does not scan 100 billion training images.

teaching.heading: Why is ten-neighbor search still expensive?
teaching.example: Choosing ten winners does not mean checking only ten candidates. With basic exact kNN, the query competes against 100 billion stored images before the ten closest are identified.

comparison.meaning: Forward cost depends on architecture and input
Different setup from the basic comparison

remember: k limits contributors to the final prediction, not necessarily the search.
Training cost and inference cost are different.
Do not assume an unspecified search acceleration.

title: Lasso and feature selection
prompt: Which performs embedded feature selection: Ridge (L2), Lasso (L1), both, or neither?
answer: B · Lasso (L1).
steps: Lasso adds λ∑|wᵢ| to the fitting loss. Its kink at zero permits solutions where some coefficients become exactly zero.
For a linear predictor, zeroing a feature’s coefficient removes its direct contribution. That sparsity is why Lasso is used for embedded feature selection.

Ridge adds λ∑wᵢ² and usually shrinks coefficients smoothly without making them exactly zero. A coefficient can be zero in a special case, but Ridge is not the standard sparsity-inducing choice. Thus “both” and “neither” miss the intended distinction.
trap: Feature scaling affects the meaning of the penalty. Correlated features can make the particular sparse selection unstable; sparse does not automatically mean causal.
recall: Why does a smaller coefficient not necessarily mean that feature has been removed?
eli5: Lasso can turn some feature knobs all the way to zero, effectively removing those inputs from a linear prediction. Ridge usually just turns the knobs down.
takeaway: L1 commonly induces exact zeros and embedded feature selection; L2 usually gives smooth shrinkage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usually shrinks coefficients rather than selecting a sparse subset.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct. Its penalty can set coefficients exactly to zero.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Not the standard distinction: L2 is not generally sparsity-inducing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Misses Lasso’s feature-selection property.

teaching.heading: Why can Lasso remove features?
teaching.example: If a feature’s coefficient is exactly zero, changing that feature cannot directly change a linear prediction. Lasso often produces those exact zeros; Ridge usually leaves small nonzero coefficients.

comparison.does: Penalty with a kink at zero

comparison.meaning: Requires zeros, not just smaller magnitudes

remember: L1 is the standard sparsity-inducing choice here.
Scale affects regularization strength across features.
Selected features need not be causal or uniquely identifiable.

title: Deriving a squared-error update
prompt: For prediction wᵀx and loss L=(y−wᵀx)², derive the update to wᵢ with learning rate λ.
answer: A · wᵢ ← wᵢ + 2λxᵢ(y−wᵀx).
steps: Let e=y−wᵀx. By the chain rule, ∂L/∂wᵢ = 2e·(−xᵢ) = −2xᵢ(y−wᵀx).
Gradient descent subtracts the derivative: wᵢ ← wᵢ−λ(−2xᵢe)=wᵢ+2λxᵢe. This accounts for both the sign and the factor of two.
For x=3, y=5, w=1, λ=0.05, the gradient is −12 and the new weight is 1.6. There is no regularization term in the stated loss, so options that insert ‖w‖² into the update are unsupported.
trap: A loss of ½(y−wᵀx)² would cancel the factor of two. Always read the loss definition before differentiating; λ here is a learning rate.
recall: Recompute the scalar example with the half-squared loss and explain the difference.
eli5: If the prediction is too small, increase weights that multiply positive inputs; if it is too large, move the other way. The derivative tells exactly how much each input contributes to that direction.
takeaway: Differentiate the stated loss, then subtract the gradient. The unhalved squared loss contributes a factor of 2.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Correct. The minus sign from the residual derivative cancels the subtraction in gradient descent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The same update plus a squared-weight-norm term
choices.explanation: Adds an unsupported term; no regularization was specified.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A residual update without the factor 2, plus a norm term
choices.explanation: Both changes are unsupported by the given loss.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Ignores how wrong the prediction is and the squared-loss derivative.

teaching.heading: Why does gradient descent add the residual term?
teaching.example: With x=3, y=5, w=1, the prediction is 3, too low by 2. The derivative is 2(3−5)×3=−12. Subtracting 0.05×(−12) raises w to 1.6, moving the prediction to 4.8.
remember: Subtracting a negative derivative increases the weight.
The unhalved squared loss contributes a factor 2.
Do not invent a regularization term absent from the loss.

title: A squared parameter restricts slope
prompt: With unlimited data, compare A: y=w²x and B: y=wx. Which can fit some datasets better?
answer: B · There are datasets where B performs better than A.
steps: The effective slope of A is a=w², so A can represent only nonnegative slopes. Model B has an unconstrained real slope and includes all of A’s predictors.
For the noiseless relationship y=−x, B chooses w=−1 and fits perfectly. No real w in A can produce slope −1.

For a positive-slope relationship, such as y=4x, A can choose w=±2 and B can choose w=4. A never has a better best-achievable fit merely from this restriction; C and D therefore do not describe the general relationship.
trap: Compare the set of possible predictions, not whether the parameter appears in a nonlinear expression. w²x is still linear in x. Unlimited data does not itself guarantee successful optimization.
recall: Give a slope that both models can represent and one that only B can represent.
eli5: Squaring the slope knob means you can never make the slope negative. An ordinary slope knob can turn either way, so it can fit every line the squared knob can fit and some extra ones.
takeaway: Compare representable slopes: w²≥0, whereas w can be any real number.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some datasets favor A over B
choices.explanation: Not in best-achievable fit: B includes every slope A can represent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some datasets favor B over A
choices.explanation: Correct. A negative-slope relationship can be fitted by B but not A.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The first is false under ideal fitting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They perform equally on all datasets
choices.explanation: False because A cannot represent negative slopes.

teaching.heading: Why is the squared-slope model more restricted?
teaching.example: To fit y=−x, model B chooses w=−1. Model A would need w²=−1, impossible for a real w. Both can fit y=4x, because A can choose w=2 and B can choose w=4.

comparison.does: Effective slope can be any real number

comparison.meaning: Does not erase a representational restriction

remember: Compare possible functions, not the appearance of a parameter formula.
A is linear in x despite using w².
Best-achievable fit and optimization success are different.

title: Different parameterizations, same slopes
prompt: Now compare A: y=(tan(w)+w)x and B: y=wx, assuming unlimited data.
answer: D · They have the same best-achievable predictions under ideal fitting.
steps: Both predictors are linear in x. The question is whether A’s effective slope a(w)=tan(w)+w can cover every real slope.
On the interval (−π/2,π/2), a(w) is continuous and strictly increasing because a′(w)=sec²(w)+1>0. Its limits at the two ends are −∞ and +∞. Hence every real slope occurs on that interval.
B also represents every real slope, so their function classes match. Neither has a representational advantage on any dataset under the intended idealized comparison.
trap: Equal function classes do not mean identical training dynamics. A has tangent singularities and different curvature; practical finite-step optimization can differ even with unlimited data.
recall: Why does a nonlinear function of the parameter not necessarily create a nonlinear function of the input?
eli5: The knob looks more complicated, but it still sets just one line’s slope. On a suitable tangent interval, tan(w)+w sweeps through every possible slope, just as a plain real-valued w does.
takeaway: A complicated parameter formula does not necessarily change the set of functions representable in the input.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Some datasets favor A over B
choices.explanation: No representational advantage: both span all real slopes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some datasets favor B over A
choices.explanation: Also no representational advantage under ideal fitting.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Neither holds as a best-achievable-function-class comparison.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They perform equally on all datasets
choices.explanation: Intended correct answer under ideal optimization; practical optimization dynamics can differ.

teaching.heading: Why can different formulas represent the same lines?
teaching.example: On (−π/2,π/2), tan(w)+w increases continuously from −infinity to +infinity. That means you can set any real slope, even though the knob is more awkward than a plain w.

comparison.meaning: Can represent every line through the origin

remember: Same function class means equal best-achievable fit.
Nonlinear in the parameter is not necessarily nonlinear in the input.
The ideal comparison does not guarantee identical SGD outcomes.

title: What is an outlier?
prompt: Which definition best describes an outlier?
answer: B · An observation that differs substantially from other observations.
steps: An outlier is unusual relative to the dataset or an assumed pattern. For measurements clustered near 10, a value near 100 could be an outlier.
It may reflect a real rare event, a different population, or a measurement error. An error is one possible explanation, not the definition.
A therefore narrows the meaning too much. C describes an ordinary observation and D a common value, so neither captures unusualness.
trap: Outlier status depends on the features, scale, and reference population. Do not automatically delete unusual but valid observations.
recall: Why might the same value be ordinary in one dataset and an outlier in another?
eli5: An outlier is the person standing far from the rest of the group. They might be there for a good reason; unusual does not automatically mean mistaken.
takeaway: An outlier is an unusually different observation, not necessarily a data error.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: One possible cause, not the definition.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A point that differs significantly from other observations
choices.explanation: Correct. It is unusual relative to the reference dataset or pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A point in the normal range
choices.explanation: Describes an ordinary observation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Describes a common observation, not an outlier.

teaching.heading: Why is an outlier not automatically an error?
teaching.example: Most temperatures near 20°C with one near 100°C look unusual. That value might be a broken sensor—or a real reading from a much hotter location. The data point is unusual before its cause is known.
remember: Outlier is a relative description.
Investigate unusual observations before deleting them.
Feature scales and reference populations matter.

title: kNN outlier scores
prompt: How does a nearest-neighbor approach identify outliers?
answer: B · They tend to have low local neighbor density.
steps: Compute the distance to a point’s kth nearest neighbor, or an average distance to its k nearest neighbors. Large distances indicate that few observations lie nearby.
For example, a point with nearest-neighbor distances 8,9,10 is more isolated than one with distances 0.1,0.2,0.3, under the same feature scaling and metric.

High density and close similarity to neighbors describe typical points. Being far from the global center is not required: an observation can be locally isolated even when a global-center test is misleading.
trap: Raw kNN-distance scores can struggle when legitimate clusters have very different densities. Normalize features and distinguish local-neighborhood reasoning from a single global mean.
recall: How would changing one feature from meters to millimeters affect unscaled Euclidean-distance scores?
eli5: If you have to walk a long way to find a point’s neighbors, that point lives in a sparse part of the dataset. Sparse neighborhoods are evidence of unusualness.
takeaway: Large nearest-neighbor distances indicate low local density and can serve as outlier scores.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Usually indicates a typical crowded region.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Correct. Isolated points have few nearby neighbors.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A global center does not define local isolation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Usually suggests the point is locally ordinary.

teaching.heading: Why do distant neighbors suggest an outlier?
teaching.example: One point’s nearest neighbors are 0.1,0.2,0.3 units away; another’s are 8,9,10 units away. Under the same scaling and metric, the second point is much more isolated.

comparison.does: Measures distance from one central summary
comparison.meaning: Not the same as local isolation

remember: kNN outlier scores often use kth-neighbor or average-neighbor distance.
Scale features before distance comparisons.
Different legitimate cluster densities can complicate interpretation.

title: Circular boundaries and VC dimension
prompt: A classifier assigns class 0 inside a learned disk and class 1 outside. What is the minimum number of distinct points that can make perfect fitting impossible?
answer: Printed C · 4 for the intended VC-dimension threshold; literally, 3 collinear points already suffice.
steps: Under the usual VC-dimension interpretation, disks in the plane have VC dimension 3: there exists a three-point configuration that can realize every labeling, whereas no four-point configuration can realize every labeling. The expected threshold is therefore 4.

For four points at (−1,−1), (1,1), (−1,1), (1,−1), label the first diagonal class 0 and the other diagonal class 1. A disk containing both points of the first diagonal cannot exclude both of the other diagonal. The opposite pairs have the same summed squared distance to any proposed center.

But the literal question asks for any distinct configuration. Use three collinear points (−1,0), (0,0), (1,0), label the endpoints 0 and the middle 1. A disk is convex, so a disk containing both endpoints also contains their midpoint. Two distinct points can always realize any labeling, making the literal minimum 3.
trap: VC dimension is an existence statement about a shatterable set, not a guarantee that every three-point configuration is shatterable. The archived wording omits a geometric assumption.
recall: Explain why the collinear counterexample does not contradict VC dimension 3.
pages: Supplemental geometric derivation; not directly taught in the supplied review
note: Wording issue: 4 for the intended VC interpretation; 3 for the literal minimum.
specificTopic: Circular classifiers, convexity, and VC dimension
eli5: A disk is filled in. If it covers two ends of a straight segment, it must cover the middle too. So three collinear points labeled inside–outside–inside already break the literal question, even though the intended VC-dimension threshold is four.
takeaway: VC dimension 3 means some three-point set can be shattered, not that every three-point set can be.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Any labels on two distinct points can be represented by a disk.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Literal minimum: collinear endpoints inside and midpoint outside cannot be fitted.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Printed answer for the intended VC-dimension threshold, with the missing geometric interpretation supplied.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Not minimal under either reading.

teaching.heading: Why does the geometry change the minimum?
teaching.example: Place three points on a line and demand that both ends be inside the disk but the middle be outside. A filled disk cannot do that. The usual “four” answer instead refers to the shattering threshold associated with VC dimension 3.

comparison.does: Any distinct point configuration can be chosen
Some 3-point set can realize every labeling
comparison.meaning: Dimension is 3; intended next threshold is 4

remember: A disk is convex.
VC dimension is about the largest shatterable set, not every set of that size.
The printed question needs a geometric qualification.

title: Zero training MSE is not a guarantee
prompt: If training MSE is zero, must test error or true error on arbitrary new data also be zero?
answer: D · Neither guarantee follows.
steps: MSE is an average of nonnegative squared residuals. Zero training MSE means every included training target is matched exactly.
That statement concerns only the observed training examples. A sufficiently flexible model can memorize them and behave badly elsewhere, especially with noise or a distribution shift.
Therefore A and B each assert more than the premise establishes. C combines two unsupported guarantees; D correctly rejects both.
trap: Training error, held-out test error, and expected population risk are different quantities. A finite test score is itself an estimate, not certainty about every future observation.
recall: Construct two functions that agree on a finite training set but differ at a new input.
specificTopic: Training error versus test and population risk
eli5: Getting every practice problem right does not guarantee getting the real exam right. Zero training error only tells you what happened on the examples used to fit the model.
takeaway: A perfect training fit does not guarantee zero test error or zero population risk.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unsupported: the test examples may reveal errors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True error on arbitrary data must be zero
choices.explanation: Unsupported: fitting observed examples does not determine all unseen behavior.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Combines two claims that do not follow.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Correct. Zero training MSE is only a statement about the training examples.

teaching.heading: Why does zero training MSE prove so little about test error?
teaching.example: A model can copy every entry in its practice folder and still guess badly on a new entry. Zero training MSE tells you every training residual is zero; it says nothing by itself about unseen residuals.

comparison.meaning: Not guaranteed by a finite perfect fit

remember: Training, test, and population error are different.
Zero squared-error average means every training residual is zero.
It does not establish a universal accuracy guarantee.

title: Counting a 4→8→2 MLP
prompt: An MLP has 4 inputs, one hidden layer with 8 units, and 2 outputs. Ignore biases and activation parameters.
answer: A · 48 weights.
steps: Input-to-hidden weights: 4×8 = 32. Each of the eight hidden units reads all four inputs.
Hidden-to-output weights: 8×2 = 16. Each of the two outputs reads all eight hidden values.
Total: 32+16 = 48. The input values and hidden activations are computed quantities, not additional learnable weights. If biases were included, they would add 8+2=10, giving 58.
trap: Count connections between successive layers, not the total number of neurons. The explicit bias exclusion matters.
recall: If the output width were 3 instead of 2, what would the bias-free weight count be?
eli5: Count wires between layers: four inputs send wires to eight hidden units, then those eight send wires to two outputs. Neuron values themselves are not extra trainable wires.
takeaway: For a bias-free dense network, sum input width × output width for each adjacent layer pair.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Undercounts the two-output connection matrix.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Does not include all connections in both matrices.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Counts hidden units, not learned connections.

teaching.heading: Why are there 48 weights?
teaching.example: Each of eight hidden units reads four inputs: 8×4=32 wires. Each of two outputs reads eight hidden values: 2×8=16 more wires. Add them for 48.
remember: Count connections rather than neurons.
Sum adjacent-layer products.
Including biases would add 8+2, giving 58.

title: An MLP without activations
prompt: A network has a hidden layer but no hidden or output activation. Which listed relationship can it represent: x, |x|, or x²?
answer: A · y=x.
steps: Without nonlinear activations, the composition is y=W₂W₁x, or an affine map if biases are allowed. More hidden units do not change that basic form.

The identity y=x is linear and therefore representable. Absolute value changes slope at zero; x² has changing slope throughout its domain, so a single affine map cannot equal either across a general domain.

The prompt says two inputs but writes scalar candidate functions. Interpret x as the relevant scalar coordinate (the other coordinate can receive weight zero), or identity component as intended. This notation mismatch does not alter the linearity argument.
trap: On a restricted finite set, an affine function might accidentally match nonlinear targets. The answer concerns representing the general relationship, including both sides of zero for |x|.
recall: Why would |x| become representable if two ReLU hidden units were introduced?
eli5: Adding more straight-line layers is like repeating instructions that only stretch and shift: the final instruction can still be written as one stretch-and-shift rule. It cannot create a bend like absolute value or a curve like a square.
takeaway: Without nonlinear activations, extra hidden units and layers still give only an affine map.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Correct. The identity is linear and can be represented.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Cannot be represented over positive and negative inputs by one affine rule.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A genuinely curved relationship over a general domain cannot be one affine map.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Incorrect because absolute value requires a slope change at zero.

teaching.heading: Why cannot a hidden layer alone create a bend?
teaching.example: If h=3x and y=2h, then y=6x: still a straight line. To represent |x| across both signs, the rule must change slope at zero; a stack without activations cannot do that.

comparison.does: Different slopes on opposite sides of zero
comparison.meaning: Needs nonlinearity over the general domain

remember: Width does not replace nonlinearity.
Composed affine maps remain affine.
Restricted finite examples can accidentally hide this limitation.

title: Why hard 0/1 loss cannot guide ordinary SGD
prompt: Can backpropagation and ordinary SGD train directly with hard 0/1 classification loss, even if the undefined threshold derivative is set aside?
answer: B · The intended obstacle is zero gradient almost everywhere.
steps: For a true positive-class example, suppose prediction is positive when score s≥0. The hard mistake loss is 1 for s<0 and 0 for s≥0.

Moving s from −2 to −1 improves the score but leaves the loss at 1. Its derivative is zero on both flat regions; only the threshold has a jump. Assigning a derivative at that jump does not provide a useful gradient across the flat regions.

Backpropagation propagates those zero local derivatives, and ordinary gradient-driven updates have no useful direction. Training commonly uses a surrogate such as cross-entropy, while 0/1 loss remains an evaluation measure.
trap: If “magically differentiable” means replacing the whole function with a useful smooth surrogate or inventing a custom nonzero gradient, the setup has changed. The keyed B applies to the hard loss with its flat regions retained.
recall: Why can a better real-valued score leave the hard mistake count unchanged?
note: Interpretation: B assumes the flat regions of hard 0/1 loss are retained.
eli5: A score can improve from “very wrong” to “almost right,” but a pass/fail light stays red until the boundary is crossed. A flat red light gives no local direction for improving the score.
takeaway: Hard 0/1 loss is flat almost everywhere; use a useful surrogate loss for ordinary gradient-based training.
